mechanism: IRIS encodes visual frames into discrete tokens via a learned autoencoder, then an autoregressive Transformer predicts subsequent token sequences, rewards, and episode termination conditioned on the entire history of tokens and actions. Because the Transformer attends over the full context rather than compressing history into a fixed latent state, it maintains coherent multi-step world-model predictions. A policy trained exclusively on these imagined rollouts thereby acquires useful behaviors without additional environment interactions.
invariant: Discrete tokenization of observations plus full-context autoregressive sequence modeling preserves multi-step predictive coherence across diverse visual environments, independent of specific game dynamics or reward structure.
prediction: Substituting the autoregressive Transformer with an RNN of equal parameter count, while keeping the discrete autoencoder identical, will measurably increase world-model prediction error over horizons longer than ~10 steps and reduce mean human-normalized score on Atari 100k under the same interaction budget.
failure_mode: If the discrete autoencoder's codebook undergoes collapse—mapping many visually distinct frames to identical tokens—the Transformer receives ambiguous inputs, making accurate next-token prediction impossible regardless of model capacity or training duration.
source_excerpt: IRIS, a data-efficient agent that learns in a world model composed of a discrete autoencoder and an autoregressive Transformer. With the equivalent of only two hours of gameplay in the Atari 100k benchmark, IRIS achieves a mean human normalized score of 1.046, and outperforms humans on 10 out of 26 games.
